proposals.name: Pinpoint statutory or regulatory authority challenge
proposals.instruction: Score whether the comment argues that the proposal exceeds, conflicts with, or misreads a specific source of legal authority, and how tightly that argument is anchored to cited text. 10 = names the statute, public law section, or CFR provision by citation, states what it actually requires, and shows the specific way the proposal departs from it. 5 = a real legal argument (for example 'the agency already has this power' or 'this exceeds the enabling act') but with the provision named only loosely and no tracking of its text. 0 = no legal-authority claim at all, or a bare adjective such as 'illegal' or 'unauthorized' with nothing cited and no reasoning behind it.
proposals.rationale: R03 argues the rule is not authorized by 7 U.S.C. §§ 7411-7425 and is redundant given the Secretary's existing plenary oversight under 7 C.F.R. § 1206.70. R59 walks 33 U.S.C. §§ 1251(b), 1341 and 1370 to argue the proposal encroaches on authority reserved to certifying states. R48 traces the 'transit bus' definition back through Pub. L. 112-141 § 32702(6) into 49 C.F.R. § 571.227. All three are dense_high_card_low. A bank built from surface features of a well-formed comment letter cannot separate these from R38 and R39, which are equally formal, equally correctly addressed, and make no authority argument at all.

proposals.name: Textual defect located together with operable replacement language
proposals.instruction: Composite. First, does the comment isolate a specific word, definition, threshold, applicability list, or paragraph of the proposed text and show what it wrongly captures or omits? Second, does it supply the correction in a form a drafter could adopt? 10 = both: the defective text is quoted or cited by section, the mis-coverage is spelled out with its practical consequence, and specific replacement or amending language is offered. 5 = the defect is precisely located but the fix is left entirely to the agency, or a fix is offered without showing what is wrong with the current text. 0 = a general complaint that the rule is too broad, too vague, or badly worded, with no located text and no proposed language.
proposals.rationale: R54 asks that Prop. Treas. Reg. § 1.861-18(f)(2)(ii) be amended and states what the amended provision should say. R48 quotes the use-based 'transit bus' definition, shows that physically identical buses land on opposite sides of it, and asks for a physical-characteristics refinement. The instructive contrast is R53, dense_low_card_high, which correctly spots that the NPRM 'casts too wide a net' and then says only that 'a simple few word changes in the NPRM are needed' without ever saying which words. R25 likewise identifies a real question about the reporting change and supplies no alternative.

proposals.name: Situates the proposal in the history of the rules it would change
proposals.instruction: Score whether the comment reasons from the trajectory of prior rules, prior agency positions, or prior versions of the same requirement. 10 = names the earlier rule, measure, or regime, states what problem it was adopted to solve, and argues concretely that this proposal would resurrect that problem or discard a solution that is currently working. 5 = mentions rulemaking history as background but the argument does not depend on it. 0 = treats the proposal as if it had no antecedents; nothing in the text indicates the commenter knows what preceded it.
proposals.rationale: R07 argues that EPA's 2020 Section 401 rule resolved problems accumulated since before the 1972 Clean Water Act and structures its entire comment around whether the new proposal re-creates them. R30 reasons from the Hatch-Waxman regime and Orange Book listings into what the BPCIA 'deemed to be a license' transition would unsettle for products already in development. R51 opposes removing an existing reporting measure by arguing what that measure currently accomplishes. All are dense_high_card_low. Historical situating leaves almost no per-sentence surface trace, so a criterion bank scoring sentences for evidence, clarity, or specificity will miss it entirely.

proposals.name: First-hand operational or casework facts the agency does not already have
proposals.instruction: Score how much of the comment consists of specific facts drawn from the commenter's own operations, records, practice, or client work, as opposed to facts any informed party could restate. 10 = concrete particulars only this commenter could supply -- named facilities and the regulations they operate under, what was tried and what happened, what their clients actually encounter -- and those particulars carry the argument. 5 = a general claim of experience ('our members operate...') with no particulars attached to any specific point. 0 = no first-hand material; the whole factual basis is background, second-hand reporting, or general knowledge.
proposals.rationale: R16 describes six clearance locations operated under 19 CFR 128 handling thousands of daily import shipments, and reasons from that operational base to the effect of the fee-announcement timing. R36 recounts which aerospace parts Boeing has already requalified for aqueous degreasing and which remain technically infeasible after years of effort. R52 describes what happens to its own clients when MTF debts are referred to Treasury for benefit offset and wage garnishment. All dense_high_card_low. R09, dense_low_card_high, opens with comparable institutional credentials (13,800 dermatologists, one in four Americans) but its supporting material never descends below general advocacy.

proposals.name: Implementation feasibility shown rather than asserted
proposals.instruction: Score whether burden, infeasibility, or benefit claims are backed by implementation detail a reader could check. 10 = states what compliance would actually require: alternatives already attempted and why they failed, qualification or testing lead times, the sequencing of the requirement against fixed external deadlines. 5 = a plausible mechanism is described but with no timeline, cost, attempt history, or dependency named. 0 = burden or benefit asserted as a bare conclusion ('burdensome', 'extra work', 'efficiencies would improve') with nothing behind it.
proposals.rationale: R36 states that the 18-month and 2-year windows are inadequate and earns that by describing the multi-year requalification program already completed for most detail parts and the residual parts with no viable alternative. R55 asks the agency to bifurcate the rule specifically because the H-1B cap season begins in about two months and employers must know the registration rules first. Both dense_high_card_low. Against them, R20 ('burdensome with no conservation gains'), R25 ('concerned about the extra work'), and R13 ('efficiencies would improve while reducing expenses') are all dense_low_card_high and assert burden or savings with no implementation content whatsoever. A rubric item asking only whether the comment addresses burden credits all five equally.

proposals.name: Consequences traced to a named affected population
proposals.instruction: Score whether the comment identifies who is affected beyond the commenter and traces the causal channel to them. 10 = names a specific population and walks the chain from the regulatory change to the effect, with at least one link that could be independently checked. 5 = names an affected group but the connection is asserted in a single step. 0 = effects described only for the commenter, or invoked for 'everyone', 'the public', or 'future generations' with no channel of any kind.
proposals.rationale: R16 runs fee-announcement timing to clearance delays to added cost to consumer prices. R24 identifies vulnerable road users, gives the fatality rate in large-truck crashes, and states the specific mechanism side guards address. R52 identifies low-income emergency patients and the precise route -- Treasury offset, tax refund offset, administrative wage garnishment -- by which the MTF/CTF misalignment reaches them. All dense_high_card_low. R60 and R10, both dense_low_card_high, invoke the general public and future generations with no traced channel at all, yet read as public-interest comments to any bank that credits stakeholder-impact language.

proposals.name: Quantitative content that bears on the specific choice before the agency
proposals.instruction: Composite of presence and relevance. 10 = supplies figures, series, or program data that speak directly to the threshold, volume, rate, or scope the agency must actually set, whether original to the commenter or drawn from an identified dataset. 5 = relevant numbers appear but are decorative and never connected to the action requested. 0 = no quantitative content, or numbers that are accurate general background about the subject matter and could be attached unchanged to any comment on the topic.
proposals.rationale: R01, under badly mangled text extraction, is a fifteen-year program dataset of project-worksheet counts and funding shares broken out at exactly the two candidate large-project threshold amounts the rule concerns. R19 asks for specific volume changes: 13.8 billion gallons, at least 390 million gallons, at least 1.2 billion gallons. R24 supplies effect sizes (55-75 percent and 20-29 percent fatality reduction) tied precisely to the cost-benefit analysis it asks NHTSA to redo. All dense_high_card_low. Contrast R10, dense_low_card_high, whose figures (50 percent of reefs lost, 25 percent of marine life, one-third of species at risk) are true and bear on no element of the designation.

proposals.name: Sources on point and claims no wider than their support
proposals.instruction: Composite. Judge (a) whether cited material actually bears on the question the proposal raises and (b) whether the comment's assertions stay inside what that material can support. 10 = identified, checkable sources squarely about the regulated question, claims scoped to them, uncertainty acknowledged where it exists. 5 = relevant sources present but one or two claims outrun them. 0 = citations that are ornamental, off-target, or unattributable, or confident causal claims the cited material cannot bear.
proposals.rationale: R47 marshals volcano emission rates, an unnamed 'group of German scientists', and a Max Planck affiliation to reach sweeping conclusions about a methane standards rule. R02 recounts wind-farm climate studies entirely at second hand and closes with 'maybe this is why bad storms in tex this year'. R33 declares the study 'fake' and lobbyist-driven with nothing behind it. All three are dense_low_card_high, which is exactly what one expects if a bank credits the presence of evidence-shaped material rather than its fit. The high end is R51, whose NSDUH prevalence figures support precisely the disparity claim being made, and R59, whose citations support precisely the federalism claim.

proposals.name: Analyzes who the rule as written would advantage, and by what mechanism
proposals.instruction: Score whether the comment reasons about incentives, capture, or abuse potential created by the proposal itself. 10 = names the interested party, identifies the specific provision that hands it leverage, and explains the mechanism by which that leverage would be exercised. 5 = raises a conflict-of-interest or misuse concern in general terms without locating it in a provision. 0 = no incentive reasoning at all, or an accusation of bad faith with no mechanism attached.
proposals.rationale: R08 argues the removal of varietal exemptions functions as a barrier to entry engineered by the California Desert Grape Administrative Committee through AMS and USDA regulatory power, and says why that subverts the purpose of the framework. R03 argues the removal authority creates an immediate conflict of interest for board employees in every action they take, and specifies whose supervision it displaces. R18 argues the training merger joins two programs whose statutory purposes can directly conflict, with a concrete example of that conflict. All dense_high_card_low. R33, dense_low_card_high, alleges lobbyist capture and supplies no mechanism, which is the difference this criterion is meant to catch.

proposals.name: Differentiated position with a distinct reason on each side
proposals.instruction: Score whether the comment distinguishes among parts of the proposal. 10 = explicitly supports some provisions and objects to others, with a separate reason attached to each, so the agency learns where the boundary of agreement lies. 5 = a single overall position plus one qualifying remark. 0 = undifferentiated endorsement or undifferentiated rejection of the proposal as a whole.
proposals.rationale: R31 supports NHTSA's reading that prototype-only vehicles are not 'motor vehicles' within the Vehicle Safety Act and separately seeks changes elsewhere in the same proposal. R55 lists the provisions its members welcome -- start-date flexibility, codified deference, entrepreneur eligibility -- before setting out the provisions it says would cause serious disruption. Both dense_high_card_low. Against them, R39 consists of an accurate restatement of the AD followed by 'IN SUPPORT', and R56 is a long species-by-species sequence of 'DSF Agrees with these proposed changes'; both are dense_low_card_high, and R39 carries the highest card_pct in the slice.

proposals.name: Share of the text that is new information rather than restatement
proposals.instruction: Estimate what fraction of the comment's substance is content the agency did not already possess. 10 = nearly all of it: argument, data, experience, or drafting the agency could not have written for itself. 5 = roughly half restatement of the proposal, half addition. 0 = a faithful summary of the proposal, or of another commenter's position, followed by agreement or disagreement, adding nothing. Length must not earn credit; a long, accurate, well-organized paraphrase belongs at the bottom of this scale.
proposals.rationale: R56 reproduces the proposed trip limits, seasons, and allocations species by species and appends agreement to each. R39 restates what the AD would require and then supports it. R13 states only that the commenter concurs with the board president's and vice president's comments. All three are dense_low_card_high, and the first two are long and orderly while contributing nothing the agency did not write itself. The high end is R19, which contributes four specific requested actions including a mechanism -- a government-issued RIN available when RIN prices are too high -- that appears nowhere in the proposal.

proposals.name: Argument stands on its own text rather than on affiliation or deferral
proposals.instruction: Score how much of the comment's substantive weight is carried by reasoning actually present in this document. 10 = the case is made in full here; membership counts, letterhead, coalition rosters, or prior filings, where mentioned, serve only to establish standing. 5 = a partial argument leaning on an external document or another party's filing for its core. 0 = the substance lives elsewhere -- 'we concur with X's comments', 'as described in our previous letter', a roster of member organizations, a recital of credentials -- with no argument developed here. Judge the argument, not the prestige of the signatory.
proposals.rationale: R06 is largely a cover letter, a roster of member districts and cities, and a pointer to two earlier comment letters. R13 is a bare concurrence with another party's filing. R38 pairs association credentials (more than 270 companies) with a single sentence of agreement. All dense_low_card_high. The mirror image is R57, dense_high_card_low, an unaffiliated commenter with no letterhead and no membership figures who develops the entire CAP-versus-VR argument in the text itself, and R49, a self-described ordinary product user who nonetheless works through the substitute-chemistry question.

proposals.name: Substantive payload relative to length and formality
proposals.instruction: Score the density of decision-relevant content per unit of document. 10 = compact and dense, with nearly every paragraph carrying an objection, a fact, a proposed change, or a supporting reason, whether or not the document is polished. 5 = a real substantive core surrounded by an equal weight of framing. 0 = extended institutional self-description, salutations, mission statements, boilerplate appreciation, and organizational history wrapped around one or two sentences of actual position. Formatting quality, letterhead, typography, and text-extraction damage must not move this score in either direction.
proposals.rationale: R38 and R39 are immaculate, correctly addressed letters whose payload is a single sentence of agreement, and R06 and R09 spend most of their length on organizational identity and general framing; all four are dense_low_card_high. In the other direction R01 arrives as shredded extraction, and R57 and R49 are plain unstyled prose, yet each carries substantive content in nearly every line, and all three are dense_high_card_low. Any bank whose items are scored over well-formed sections of a letter will read presentational polish as substance and extraction damage as its absence.

proposals.name: Takes a position the agency can act on rather than requesting clarification
proposals.instruction: Score whether the comment gives the agency something it can adopt or reject. 10 = states a position and the reasons for it; any questions posed are in service of that position. 5 = mixes a weakly stated position with requests for information. 0 = the document consists of clarification requests, requests for lists or definitions, statements of confusion, or a request for additional time, with no position on the substance of the proposal.
proposals.rationale: R32 is a sequence of requests -- 'Provide a list specific components require failure testing', 'What proof/documentation is acceptable to demonstrate the absence of air reversal?' -- with observations embedded around them. R25 asks how the reporting change would help and says 'I'm just confused'. R27 and R44 are, in the text presented, purely requests to extend the comment period. All four are dense_low_card_high, which is what one expects if a bank credits provision-level engagement without asking whether a position was taken. The contrast is R34, which also complains of insufficient specificity but converts that into a positive argument about what Congress directed the agency to produce.

proposals.name: Engages the agency's stated rationale, and represents the proposal faithfully
proposals.instruction: Composite. Judge (a) whether the comment states the agency's own reason for the proposal and answers it on those terms, and (b) whether the proposal is represented accurately. 10 = the rationale is stated recognizably and then rebutted or extended on its own ground, with quotations used in context. 5 = argues a responsive position but never engages the stated rationale. 0 = argues past the proposal, attacks a version of it the text does not support, or assembles quotations into a contradiction that dissolves once they are read together.
proposals.rationale: R34 takes EPA's stated position that it will continue applying existing guidance and answers it directly: had Congress thought past approaches adequate it would not have directed a rule within one year. R07 states what the 2020 Rule was for and argues the proposal on exactly that ground. Both dense_high_card_low. R12 is the diagnostic failure case, dense_low_card_high: it sets 'best scientific and commercial data available' against 'exact population trends and density estimates ... are not determinable at this time' and calls them contradictory, when the first is a standard of decision and the second a description of the record -- so a comment that quotes the proposal, is carefully organized, and looks rigorous rests on a misreading. R33 attacks a study rather than the proposal's content.

proposals.name: Scan and attachment debris: OCR corruption, stubs, stray headers
proposals.instruction: Reading only the comment text, score 0-10 for HOW MUCH digitization and attachment-transfer debris is visibly present, i.e. material that came from the document's route into the docket rather than from someone's keyboard. Count all of: (a) a bare pointer stub standing alone before the body, such as 'See attached file(s)', 'See Attached', 'Please see attached'; (b) character-level corruption where letters are replaced by symbols or lookalikes, words are split mid-token, or ligatures are mangled; (c) chart, axis or table text exploded into one character or fragment per line; (d) letterhead fragments, postal addresses, telephone/fax numbers, page numbers, 'Page 2', received-stamps or footnote markers interleaved into the middle of sentences; (e) heavy blank-line padding between lines. Anchors: 0 = continuous clean prose with none of this; 3 = a pointer stub plus a few stray header lines; 7 = frequent corrupted words and interleaved page furniture; 10 = most lines are debris rather than sentences. Do NOT judge whether the debris makes the comment better or worse, do NOT try to reconstruct or evaluate the underlying document, and do NOT infer anything about the author's care or competence. Report only the visible extent.
proposals.rationale: MODE 1 surface feature with a MODE 2 parent named for honesty. Debris volume tracks the scanning route and the vintage of the paper, which cannot make an argument better or worse. It is loud in this slice and appears on BOTH sides, so it is exactly the kind of feature two models can weigh differently for non-substantive reasons: R07 (1980 letter, 'heolfh industry monufQcfurers QSSOCfQtlon', 'manu£acture', '1980 FEE -i> PH 2 16') and R56 (UPS, 'lowe e023 ups', 'flet', 'samme') sit on the dense_low_card_high side, while R30 (FEMA chart rendered as one letter per line) and R03 (Capespan, 'CAPES PAN', '20250-Q237', 'Capespan Grou~') sit on the dense_high_card_low side. R25 (1977 Norwich Pharmacal, '□V NopwicK Phannnacal Company') is a third heavily corrupted case.
proposals.upstream_parent: how the item entered the docket (typed in the web box vs. filed as a scanned or PDF attachment) and the age of the paper original, plus the OCR pipeline that transcribed it

proposals.name: Formal correspondence apparatus: letterhead, address block, caption, salutation, signature
proposals.instruction: Reading only the comment text, score 0-10 for HOW MUCH formal business-letter apparatus surrounds the substance. Count the presence and elaboration of: a dated letterhead or organizational address with phone/fax/URL; the recipient agency's full postal address; a transmission note ('Submitted via Email', 'VIA ELECTRONIC FILING', 'Via Docket Submission', 'Submitted electronically to http://www.regulations.gov'); an 'RE:' or 'Subject:' caption reciting the docket number, RIN and Federal Register citation; a salutation naming an individual official with an honorific and job title; a formal close with a signer's name and title; continuation headers such as 'Page 2 of 5'; and clerical residue such as typist initials. Anchors: 0 = no apparatus at all, the text begins with the substantive point; 5 = a date, a caption and a generic salutation; 10 = the full apparatus, elaborated, including named recipient, transmission note, page furniture and titled signature block. This is a count of formal packaging ONLY. Do NOT judge whether the packaging is appropriate, professional, respectful, or indicative of a serious submission, and do NOT let the substance of the letter influence the number.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2. Access to secretarial/government-affairs support determines how much of this wrapper exists, and that support is unequally distributed; the wrapper itself contains no argument. It varies enormously across the slice independently of the substantive point: R01 (ACC/CBC: full agency address, named salutation 'Dear Ms. Jennings', footnotes, titled signature) and R47 (Sonosky law firm: four office addresses and a twenty-plus-name attorney roster) are maximal, while R12 (spearfishing carve-out) and R46 (SSI/Medicaid auto-enrollment) carry none at all. R03 even preserves typist initials ('MAG:hs') and R39 preserves 'YA:dm'. Tagged mixed because a filer with a government-affairs office may also genuinely produce better-grounded comments.
proposals.upstream_parent: institutional administrative resources behind the filing (staff, government-affairs or clerical support, house letterhead templates)

proposals.name: Sheer volume of retained body text
proposals.instruction: Reading only the comment text, score 0-10 for HOW MUCH body text there is, as a raw quantity. Judge extent by approximate word count and by structural signs of length: numbered or lettered section headings, a table of contents, roman-numeral parts, bulleted lists of asks, and page-continuation markers. Anchors: 0 = under roughly 60 words (one short paragraph); 3 = a few paragraphs; 5 = roughly one page; 8 = several pages with internal sectioning; 10 = a long multi-part document with a contents listing or many numbered sections. Do NOT reward or penalise length, do NOT judge whether the length is warranted by the subject, and do NOT consider how well the space is used. Report volume only.
proposals.rationale: MODE 1 counter with a MODE 2 parent. Length is the canonical nuisance: it is cheap for a resourced filer and expensive for an individual, and it separates the two halves of this slice almost mechanically. R12 (about 50 words) and R46 (two sentences) are dense_low_card_high; R29 (State of Colorado, multi-page with statutory sections), R52 (Monroe Energy, with an EXECUTIVE SUMMARY and bulleted asks) and R13 (which literally opens with a 'Contents ... Transcript ... List of Attendees' listing) are long documents on the dense_high_card_low side. Tagged mixed honestly: more preparation time plausibly buys genuine substance as well as bulk, so this must appear in the sensitivity band rather than being silently discounted.
proposals.upstream_parent: staff time and preparation resources invested in the submission (in-house counsel, consultants, an organization drafting over weeks vs. an individual typing at a keyboard)

proposals.name: Organizational self-introduction and constituency-scale preamble
proposals.instruction: Reading only the comment text, score 0-10 for HOW MUCH of the text is devoted to introducing the submitting body and establishing its standing before (or instead of) addressing the rule. Count: statements of who the submitter is and what it does; quantified scale claims (number of members, member companies, employees, states, countries, dues payers, shipments per day, years since founding); superlatives about position ('the largest', 'the oldest', 'the world's largest', 'premier'); descriptions of the network or affiliates the submitter belongs to or speaks for; and explanations of why the submitter is an affected or interested party. Anchors: 0 = no self-description whatsoever; 3 = a single clause naming the organization; 6 = a full paragraph of mission and membership description; 10 = multiple paragraphs, or footnotes, given over to scale, mission and standing. Do NOT assess whether the claims are true, impressive, or relevant, do NOT treat a large claimed constituency as making the comment more or less worth reading, and do NOT judge the substantive point that follows.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2. Organizational scale and reputation are classic unseen upstream factors; their textual fingerprint is the standing preamble, and the preamble carries no analysis of the rule. Present in force on both halves, so it is predictive without being substantive: R39 (ALPA, 'representing the safety interests of more than 78,000 professional airline pilots flying for 41 airlines') and R42 (AADA, 'more than 13,800 dermatologists nationwide') sit on the dense_low_card_high side, while R28 (CAPA, 'over 30,000 professional flight crewmembers'), R48 (Boeing, 'approximately 150,000 people ... more than 150 countries') and R43 (DEPA, a full page of self-description before any comment) sit on the dense_high_card_low side. R08 and R31 both open by explaining their identical P&A/CAP institutional role. Tagged mixed: a large, well-networked body may both advertise itself AND actually know more.
proposals.upstream_parent: the size, reputation and network position of the producing organization (an unobserved trait it advertises because advertising it is believed to help)

proposals.name: Legal-authority citation apparatus: statutes, Federal Register cites, footnotes
proposals.instruction: Reading only the comment text, score 0-10 for HOW DENSE the formal legal-citation apparatus is. Count occurrences of: United States Code and Code of Federal Regulations citations with section symbols; Federal Register volume-and-page citations; public-law numbers and Statutes-at-Large cites; executive-order numbers; docket numbers and RIN identifiers used as formal captions; quoted statutory language with defined-term parentheticals such as ('CWA' or 'the Act'); numbered footnotes with sources or URLs; and citation-style short forms ('See', 'citing', 'et seq.', 'Prop. Treas. Reg. Sec.'). Anchors: 0 = no citations of any kind; 3 = the docket number and nothing else; 6 = several statutory or Federal Register cites in running text; 10 = citations in most paragraphs plus a working footnote apparatus. Do NOT check whether the citations are accurate, apt, or well deployed, and do NOT treat citation as evidence that the argument is sound. Count the apparatus only.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2. Whether a comment was drafted by a lawyer is invisible, but it leaves this exact fingerprint, and the fingerprint is a drafting convention rather than an argument. On this slice it clusters almost entirely on one side of the disagreement: R29 (State of Colorado, '33 U.S.C. § 1251(b); 33 U.S.C. § 1341; 33 U.S.C. § 1370', '84 Fed. Reg. 44080'), R24 (New Flyer, 'Pub. L. 112-141 ... 126 Stat. 809', '49 C.F.R. § 571.227') and R34 (National Mango Board, '7 U.S.C. §§ 7411 - 7425', '7 C.F.R. § 1206.70') are all dense_high_card_low, as are R23 (a law firm's own letterhead filing) and R09 (footnoted federal survey sources). Tagged mixed: a party that can afford counsel may also bring a genuinely better-grounded legal argument.
proposals.upstream_parent: drafting by trained legal counsel (outside law firm or in-house regulatory lawyers) rather than by the affected party directly

proposals.name: Process-management asks about the rulemaking's conduct, not its content
proposals.instruction: Reading only the comment text, score 0-10 for HOW MUCH of the submission is addressed to the CONDUCT of the rulemaking process rather than to the regulated subject itself. Count: requests to extend or reopen the comment period; statements that the comment period was too short or fell near a holiday; requests to split, bifurcate, sequence or issue multiple final rules; requests that a requirement be moved into a different docket or proposed rule; questions about when a rule will take effect or when a revised rule will issue; requests to withdraw or re-issue the proposal without engaging its merits; and requests for a meeting or further discussion. Anchors: 0 = the text is entirely about the regulated subject; 5 = the text makes a substantive point and also one process request; 10 = the entire submission is a process request with only enough background to motivate it. Do NOT judge whether the process request is reasonable, well founded, or made in good faith. Score only how much of the text is process-management.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2. Submission timing relative to the comment deadline is invisible in the corpus, but it determines whether a filer sends a procedural placeholder or a substantive analysis; the resulting text is systematically different while the filer's underlying substantive capacity is unchanged. Two entire submissions in this slice are nothing but an extension request and both sit on the dense_low_card_high side: R01 (ACC/CBC, '30-day extension of the comment period', noting the deadline 'ends on January 4, just after the Holiday Season') and R05 (Philip Morris International, 'respectfully request that FDA extend the 90-day comment period by an additional 90 days'). The same fingerprint appears embedded elsewhere: R34 ('the one month comment period ... is much too short'), R17 ('we urge the agency to either bifurcate or issue multiple final rules'), R27 (asks that a limitation be relocated to a sibling NPRM) and R13 ('when can we anticipate the revised rules to be in effect'). Tagged not-mixed: the timing of a filing does not itself make the filer's substance better.
proposals.upstream_parent: when in the docket's life the item was produced and filed (an early, deadline-driven procedural filing vs. a later substantive one), and the filer's familiarity with docket mechanics

proposals.name: Supplied campaign wording and stock talking points
proposals.instruction: Reading only the comment text, score 0-10 for HOW MUCH of the wording reads as supplied to the writer rather than composed by the writer. Cues: sentences in polished advocacy cadence sitting inside otherwise plain or error-prone personal prose; statistics and guideline references quoted with no source and in slogan form; an explicit statement of alignment with another named organization's own filing or petition; capitalised emphasis words dropped into otherwise ordinary sentences; a first-person personal-stakes frame ('me and my family') attached to a policy ask; and a close of the form 'Sincerely,' plus a personal name and, sometimes, a home street address. Anchors: 0 = every sentence is idiosyncratic to this writer and this situation; 5 = a personally written frame around one or two obviously stock sentences; 10 = the body consists almost entirely of stock advocacy sentences with only a name changed. Do NOT judge whether the supplied wording is accurate or the position correct, and do NOT treat a templated comment as either lazy or well informed. Score only how supplied the wording looks.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2, and directly visible here. R04 and R10 are different individuals on different letters that nonetheless share near-verbatim sentences: both contain 'The 20152020 Dietary Guidelines recommends that no more than 10 percent of my calories come from added sugars' and both close with 'Given the high rates of diet-related diseases in America, the FDA should act quickly to require the new Nutrition Facts labels without the proposed delay', plus a shared 'more realistic serving sizes ... what I am likely to eat' line; R04 signs off with a full home street address. Both sit on the dense_low_card_high side. The same fingerprint appears on the other side in R15, which opens by endorsing 'the League of American Bicyclists' comments' and then recites campaign statistics with capitalised emphasis ('EVERYONE', 'ALL', 'SO MANY'), and in R51. Tagged not-mixed: the campaign's decision to mobilise says nothing about the substantive contribution of this particular submission.
proposals.upstream_parent: an organizing campaign or membership organization that drafted the language and distributed it to individual submitters

proposals.name: Alphanumeric part and service-bulletin identifier density
proposals.instruction: Reading only the comment text, score 0-10 for HOW DENSELY the text is carried by alphanumeric designators keyed to an external technical document. Count: part numbers and P/N strings; model, effectivity or configuration codes; service-bulletin, notice or revision numbers; station, figure, table, task and step references into another document; quantities written with unit codes; and itemised bullet lists whose content is mostly such strings. Anchors: 0 = no alphanumeric designators anywhere; 3 = a docket number and one model name; 6 = several designators used in running prose; 10 = most sentences contain at least one designator and the body is essentially a keyed list of them. Do NOT check whether the designators are correct, do NOT assess whether the technical point is right or important, and do NOT treat specificity as a virtue. Count the density of the strings only.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2. Sitting inside an operator's engineering department gives free access to a register that other commenters cannot produce at any price; the fingerprint is designator density, not the merit of the observation. It is strikingly concentrated on one half of this slice: R14 (International Aero Engines, 'V2522-A5, V2524-A5, V2527-A5, V2527E-A5, V2527M-A5, V2530-A5 and V2533-A5'), R22 (Jetstar, 'B787-81205-SB250291-00', 'STA 1233, 1257, and 1281', '10EA BACB30NX6K3'), R45 (Japan Airlines, 'P/N MA30A1017', 'Boeing SB 777-28A0034 Rev. 3'), R27 (Qantas, '737-71-1937 RB', 'D626A001-9-01') and R56 (UPS, 'Ipeco 3A258-004X') are all dense_low_card_high. Tagged mixed: proximity to the hardware plausibly produces genuinely more useful observations as well as more identifier strings.
proposals.upstream_parent: the author's occupational proximity to the regulated hardware (airline or operator engineering staff who hold the maintenance documents on their desk), which supplies this vocabulary at no cost to them

proposals.name: Unedited orthography: typos, run-ons, informal capitalization
proposals.instruction: Reading only the comment text, score 0-10 for HOW MANY departures from copy-edited standard written English are attributable to the writing itself (as distinct from scanning damage, which is scored separately and must be ignored here). Count: misspellings and transposed letters; missing or doubled spaces around punctuation; sentences beginning in lower case; run-on sentences and comma splices; missing sentence-final punctuation; erratic capitalisation used for emphasis; absent paragraph structure; and inconsistent spacing or line breaks inside sentences. Anchors: 0 = fully copy-edited, no errors visible; 3 = one or two slips; 6 = errors in most paragraphs; 10 = errors in most sentences, structure largely absent. Do NOT infer from errors that the writer is uninformed, careless or unserious, do NOT let the writer's position or tone affect the number, and do NOT judge the comment. Count visible writing-level departures only.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2, and the upstream factor the prompt names explicitly. Whether anyone proofread the filing is invisible, but it leaves a dense and easily scored trace. In this slice the unedited extreme is concentrated on the dense_low_card_high side: R44 ('i think you are purposely doing a fake study', 'theri body', 'govgt', 'probalby'), R53 ('maybe this is why bad storms in tex this year') and R59 ('The Nonsince of Climate change ideas', 'Maybe we can tax a volcano') are all conspicuously unedited, as against R09, R29 and R52, which are clean throughout. Tagged mixed and honestly so: a filer who can buy an editor can usually also buy an analyst, so discounting this channel risks discounting real substance and it must be carried in the sensitivity band.
proposals.upstream_parent: access to professional editing, proofreading or drafting assistance before filing

proposals.name: Narrow equipment-and-operations subject matter versus broad policy subject matter
proposals.instruction: Reading only the comment text, score 0-10 for WHERE the subject matter sits on a single axis, from broad contested public policy (0) to narrow bounded technical or administrative operations (10). Score toward 10 when the matter is a specific piece of equipment or a specific operational or administrative mechanic: an airworthiness directive or service bulletin, a part or seat or valve, a marketing-order district map or reporting form, a gear restriction or trip limit, an enrollment or certification step, a definitional carve-out for one vehicle or vessel type. Score toward 0 when the matter is a broad contested question of public policy: greenhouse-gas or emissions standards, water-quality federalism, immigration and visa programs, health-coverage or benefit design, tobacco control, endangered-species listing. Score 5 for a mixed or intermediate subject. Do NOT judge which kind of subject matters more, do NOT consider who wrote it or how well it is argued, and do NOT treat narrowness or breadth as a strength or a weakness. Place the subject on the axis and stop.
proposals.rationale: MODE 2 (corpus composition is a genuine upstream factor beyond the text, and topic words are its fingerprint) and a MODE 1 subject-matter marker. Topic alone tracks the disagreement here almost as well as anything about the writing: the narrow airworthiness cluster R14, R45, R22, R27 and R56, plus other narrow-operations items R12 (spearfishing gear), R19 (watermelon board districts) and R55 (walnut reporting), all sit on the dense_low_card_high side, while the broad-policy cluster R11 (methane standards), R29 (Clean Water Act section 401), R38, R52 and R17 (H-1B) all sit on the dense_high_card_low side. Nothing about the topic itself is a property of the comment's substantive quality, so it is a nuisance. Tagged mixed because dockets differ in the sophistication of the population that files in them, so topic may co-vary with real quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: which agency and docket the item was drawn from, i.e. the composition of the corpus and the population that habitually comments in that docket

proposals.name: Specific, implementable regulatory fix
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the comment identifies a precise provision, section, figure, table, or part number in the proposed rule or supporting document AND proposes a specific, concrete correction. A 10: pinpoints exact locations (e.g., a specific figure/table/step) and states exactly what should replace them. A 0: comment expresses only a general objection or support with no identifiable target provision and no concrete fix.
proposals.rationale: R01 (dense_pct=0.324, card_pct=0.929) and R46 (dense_pct=0.143, card_pct=0.956) are both dense_low_card_high: each pinpoints exact figures/engine-model lists to correct, and the scorecard rewards this heavily while the dense model, apparently uninterested in narrow single-issue technical corrections, ranks both near the bottom of the pool.

proposals.name: Substance-to-boilerplate ratio
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on what fraction of the visible text is actual argument/analysis versus non-substantive administrative content (letterhead, attorney/board rosters, address blocks, signature blocks, 'see attached file' notices). A 10: virtually all text is substantive argument. A 0: the great majority of visible text is letterhead, personnel lists, or contact boilerplate with little or no argument.
proposals.rationale: R03 (Sonosky law firm letter, dense_pct=0.970, card_pct=0.188) and R14 (ASSE letter, dense_pct=0.965, card_pct=0.255) are both dense_high_card_low: extensive attorney rosters and board-of-directors lists dominate the visible text before any argument appears, yet dense rates both near the top of the pool while the scorecard rates both near the bottom -- suggesting dense credits the institutional apparatus that the scorecard discounts (or fails to see past).

proposals.name: Acknowledges both merits and drawbacks
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the comment explicitly identifies both positive and negative aspects of the proposal (or explicitly frames the regulator's own competing goals) rather than arguing one-sidedly. A 10: comment clearly separates what it supports from what it opposes and explains why for each. A 0: comment is purely one-sided (all praise or all condemnation) with no acknowledgment of any countervailing consideration.
proposals.rationale: R05 (U.S. Chamber of Commerce, dense_pct=0.708, card_pct=0.100) explicitly separates 'positive developments' it welcomes from 'problematic provisions' it opposes, and R06 (Alliance for Automotive Innovation, dense_pct=0.878, card_pct=0.115) frames Congress's own balancing of competing goals before taking a position -- both dense_high_card_low, suggesting balanced argumentation is exactly the property the scorecard is missing.

proposals.name: Pinpoint statutory/regulatory citation
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the comment cites specific statutory sections, CFR provisions, or exact regulatory text (by number/subsection) that are relevant and appear accurately applied to the argument. A 10: multiple precise, correctly-used pinpoint citations integrated into the argument. A 0: no statutory/regulatory citations, or only vague references to 'the law' or 'the Act' without section numbers.
proposals.rationale: R25 (State of Colorado, dense_pct=0.898, card_pct=0.038) cites 33 U.S.C. sections 1251(b), 1341, and 1370 by number, and R09 (Eversheds Sutherland, dense_pct=0.881, card_pct=0.211) cites the exact proposed Treas. Reg. section at issue -- both dense_high_card_low, with dense ranking near the top of the pool for this legal precision while the scorecard ranks both near the bottom.

proposals.name: Attributable sourcing of statistics
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether factual/statistical claims are attributed to a specific, named, checkable source (agency report, dataset, named study with year) versus vague appeals to unnamed authority. A 10: every empirical claim is tied to a specific named source. A 0: comment makes empirical claims attributed only to vague phrases like 'researchers have found' or 'studies show' with no identifiable source.
proposals.rationale: R56 (Campaign for Tobacco-Free Kids, dense_pct=0.761, card_pct=0.025) footnotes a specific named 2021 NSDUH report yet scores near the floor on the scorecard, while R41 (dense_pct=0.301, card_pct=0.941) makes vague, unattributed 'researchers have found' claims about wind farms and scores near the ceiling -- the scorecard appears to reward citation-like phrasing rather than actual sourcing rigor.

proposals.name: Claims calibrated to evidence, no leaps
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the strength of the comment's claims matches the strength of its evidence, avoiding unsupported causal leaps, conspiratorial framing, or sweeping conclusions drawn from a single tangential fact. A 10: every claim is proportionate to and follows logically from the evidence offered. A 0: comment draws sweeping or conspiratorial conclusions (e.g., alleging a coordinated cover-up, or linking an isolated local fact to a global causal claim) without supporting logic.
proposals.rationale: R43 (dense_pct=0.383, card_pct=0.925) leaps from one volcano's CO2 output and an unnamed 'group of German scientists' to dismissing anthropogenic climate policy entirely, and R49 (dense_pct=0.264, card_pct=0.908) asserts a coordinated 'fake govt study' conspiracy without evidence -- both dense_low_card_high, with the scorecard rating both extremely high despite the reasoning failures dense (correctly) discounts.

proposals.name: Concrete organizational standing disclosed
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the commenter establishes concrete, verifiable standing relevant to the rule -- membership size, statutory mandate, years of operation, or domain expertise -- beyond a bare assertion of interest. A 10: comment states specific, concrete standing facts directly tied to the rule's subject. A 0: the commenter's relationship to and authority on the subject matter is entirely unstated or purely generic ('as a concerned citizen').
proposals.rationale: R55 (NASW, dense_pct=0.801, card_pct=0.134) opens by stating '130,000 members' and its role in LTC advocacy, and R14 (ASSE, dense_pct=0.965, card_pct=0.255) states '37,000... safety, health, and environmental professionals' -- both dense_high_card_low, suggesting dense rewards this credentialing far more than the scorecard does.

proposals.name: Identifies internal contradiction in proposal
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the comment identifies and explains a specific logical inconsistency, factual error, or internal contradiction within the proposed rule's or supporting document's own text. A 10: comment quotes or closely paraphrases two internally inconsistent statements from the proposal and explains precisely why they conflict. A 0: comment identifies no internal inconsistency in the proposal.
proposals.rationale: R48 (dense_pct=0.059, card_pct=0.665) builds its entire argument around exposing a contradiction between the proposal's claim of a 'thorough review' and its own admission that population data is incomplete, and R01 (dense_pct=0.324, card_pct=0.929) flags mismatched figure/part-number references within the same service bulletin -- both dense_low_card_high, with the scorecard crediting this demanding reasoning move far more than dense does, suggesting dense may underweight it relative to more surface-level cues like formality or letterhead.

proposals.name: States core position in opening sentences
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the comment's central request or position (support/oppose/specific ask) is clearly stated within the first two sentences, versus deferred behind extended preamble or organizational background. A 10: the specific ask or position is unambiguous from the first sentence or two. A 0: the reader must read through substantial preamble before the core position becomes clear.
proposals.rationale: R08 (ACC extension request, dense_pct=0.079, card_pct=0.830) opens by stating the exact 30-day extension request in its first line, and R39 (coral habitat comment, dense_pct=0.197, card_pct=0.793) opens 'I strongly SUPPORT...' as its first sentence -- both dense_low_card_high, with the scorecard rewarding this immediacy far above where dense ranks it.

proposals.name: Itemized engagement with discrete provisions
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the comment is organized into discrete, clearly delineated points (numbered list, bullets, per-provision headers) that each address a distinct aspect of the proposal, versus one undifferentiated block of prose covering multiple issues. A 10: comment is clearly segmented so each distinct issue gets its own clearly marked point. A 0: multiple issues are conflated within a single continuous unsegmented paragraph structure.
proposals.rationale: R42 (fisheries comment, dense_pct=0.224, card_pct=0.862) responds species-by-species with agree/disagree bullets, and R54 (biosafety HVAC comment, dense_pct=0.004, card_pct=0.728) poses numbered, page-referenced technical questions on distinct components -- both dense_low_card_high, and R54 in particular sits near the very bottom of the dense ranking despite its meticulous structure, suggesting dense discounts itemized engagement that the scorecard rewards.

proposals.name: Traces concrete downstream compliance consequence
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the comment explains a specific, concrete operational or compliance consequence that would follow from the rule as drafted -- who is affected, how, and by what mechanism -- rather than a general objection. A 10: comment traces a clear causal chain from the rule's specific text to a concrete real-world consequence for an identified party. A 0: comment states only that the rule is good/bad/burdensome without explaining any mechanism or affected party.
proposals.rationale: R27 (New Flyer, dense_pct=0.889, card_pct=0.042) explains how a poorly-worded definition subjects physically identical transit buses to inconsistent rollover requirements, and R31 (FedEx, dense_pct=0.884, card_pct=0.186) explains how specific fee-timing provisions translate into increased costs and shipment delays for identified customers -- both dense_high_card_low, with dense ranking both near the top of the pool for this consequence-tracing while the scorecard ranks both near the bottom.

proposals.name: First-hand operational evidence for claims
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the comment's claims are grounded in the filer's own direct first-hand operational, technical, or field experience (their own fleet, lab, cases, data) rather than generic policy assertions. A 10: comment clearly draws on specific first-hand experience the filer possesses and describes it concretely. A 0: comment consists entirely of generic assertions with no indication of direct first-hand experience.
proposals.rationale: R02 (Japan Airlines, dense_pct=0.139, card_pct=0.918) grounds its argument in JAL's own actuator-installation timeline experience, and R34 (a USGS biologist's peer-review email on the Iiwi status report, dense_pct=0.080, card_pct=0.724) cites specific field studies and corrects specific sentences from direct expertise -- both dense_low_card_high, with dense ranking both near the very bottom of the pool despite the scorecard recognizing their substance, suggesting dense may discount genuine first-hand expertise when it arrives in an unpolished or informal register (a technical bulletin excerpt; a casual email) rather than formal advocacy prose.

proposals.name: Filer-specific detail vs generic boilerplate
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the comment contains concrete, filer-specific details (named local programs, actual case/client experience, jurisdiction-specific facts) that could not be copy-pasted unchanged into a comment on an unrelated docket, versus fully generic advocacy language. A 10: comment is saturated with details unique to this filer's specific situation. A 0: comment reads as entirely generic and interchangeable, with nothing identifying who is writing or their particular circumstances.
proposals.rationale: R53 (Utah Disability Law Center, dense_pct=1.000, card_pct=0.284) ties its argument to its named relationship with NDRN and its specific CAP program, while R18 (dense_pct=0.807, card_pct=0.103) makes a nearly identical argument about the same rule with no organizational identity or jurisdiction-specific detail at all -- both dense_high_card_low, and the scorecard barely differentiates them (0.284 vs 0.103) despite the large difference in filer-specific grounding, suggesting this dimension is missing from the scorecard's bank entirely.

proposals.name: Engages the rule's actual operative text
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the comment engages with the specific operative mechanics of the proposed rule (the actual provision, exemption, standard, or requirement at issue) versus expressing general sentiment about the broader topic area untethered to what the rule specifically does. A 10: comment is clearly anchored to the specific mechanism the proposed rule would create or change. A 0: comment expresses general topic-area sentiment without referencing what the specific proposal actually does.
proposals.rationale: R45 (Boeing, dense_pct=0.981, card_pct=0.228, dense_high_card_low) is deeply anchored in the specific TCE vapor-degreasing prohibition, its timeline, and the lack of a qualified alternative, while R26 (dense_pct=0.169, card_pct=0.730, dense_low_card_high) is generic 'protect the ocean' sentiment that never engages the specific fishing-gear exemption under review -- dense correctly separates these (very high vs. low) while the scorecard rates the generic comment far higher than the specifically-engaged one, exactly inverting what should distinguish them.

proposals.name: Internally consistent, labeled quantitative detail
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether numeric figures in the comment (dollar amounts, dates, volumes, percentages, thresholds) are clearly labeled, tied to a specific claim, and internally consistent with each other, versus numbers appearing without clear labels or context. A 10: every number is clearly labeled, its meaning is unambiguous, and figures are internally consistent. A 0: numbers appear disconnected from any clear label or claim, making it impossible to tell what they refer to or whether they are consistent.
proposals.rationale: R51 (Monroe Energy, dense_pct=0.939, card_pct=0.157, dense_high_card_low) ties every figure ('13.8 billion gallons,' '390 million gallons,' '1.2 billion gallons') to a specific, clearly-labeled ask, which the scorecard entirely fails to reward. R12 (dense_pct=0.804, card_pct=0.128, dense_high_card_low) is a dense wall of dollar figures and percentages stripped of labels by OCR extraction, uninterpretable as presented -- dense rates it almost as highly as R51's cleanly-labeled figures, suggesting dense may be responding to the surface presence of quantitative data without verifying it is actually interpretable, a distinction this criterion would sharpen.

proposals.name: Overall word-count / length of submission
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate ONLY how long this comment is (extent of raw length/word count), where 0 = extremely short (a sentence or two) and 10 = very long (multiple pages of dense text). Do NOT judge whether the length is appropriate, excessive, or a mark of quality -- score length alone.
proposals.rationale: Length is a strong surface confound in this slice: dense-favored items (R02 NFTC letter, R11 Boeing letter, R14 NHA letter) run to multi-page corporate submissions truncated at the read window, while card-favored items (R07 spearfishing carve-out, R13 Nantucket habitat plea, R19 watermelon board note) are one short paragraph. Length tracks who has staff time to draft, not argument quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: institutional resources / staff time available to draft

proposals.name: Formal business-letter salutation and closing conventions
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the comment follows formal business-letter conventions -- e.g. a 'Dear ___:' salutation, a 'Re:' or 'RE:' subject line, and a formal complimentary close such as 'Sincerely,' followed by a printed name/title. 0 = none of these conventions present, 10 = all of these conventions fully present. Do NOT judge whether this formality is appropriate or a sign of a good comment -- score only the presence/extent of the convention.
proposals.rationale: Formal salutation/close conventions co-occur heavily with dense-favored items (R02's 'Dear Sirs:'/'Sincerely'; R50's 'To Whom It May Concern'/'Re:') and are almost absent from card-favored personal comments (R07, R13, R26), making this a genre marker rather than a quality marker.

proposals.name: Attachment cover-note opener ('see attached file')
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the comment text begins with a short cover-note phrase indicating the substantive content is/was a separately attached file (e.g. 'See attached', 'Please find attached', 'Attached is...') before or instead of any pasted document body. 0 = no such cover-note phrase, 10 = the item consists almost entirely of this cover-note phrase with an obvious separate pasted-attachment block. Do NOT judge whether attaching a file is a good practice -- score only the extent of this pattern.
proposals.rationale: Several dense-favored items open with a bare cover-note before the real document ('Please find attached the comments of Eversheds Sutherland' R03; 'Please see attached for comments from The Boeing Company' R11; 'Attached is the Alliance for Automotive Innovation comment' R12), an artifact of how the item was uploaded to the portal, unrelated to the substance of the attached comment.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission channel (file-upload vs. direct textbox entry)

proposals.name: OCR/scan transcription artifacts and garbled text
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the text shows signs of being transcribed from a scanned document via OCR -- e.g. misrecognized characters, run-together or reversed letters (like 'Woter' for 'Water', 'flet' for 'fleet'), missing spaces, or nonsensical character substitutions. 0 = clean, obviously machine-typed text with no such artifacts, 10 = pervasive garbling throughout. Do NOT judge whether this hurts readability or comment quality -- score only the extent of the transcription artifacts.
proposals.rationale: OCR garbling is concentrated in older/scanned submissions and correlates with card-favored outcomes independent of content: R06 (UPS Airlines, 'flet', 'the samme'), R09 ('Woter', 'ltr/ater'), R31 (chart/table OCR dump of a bar-graph), R59 (1977 Norwich Pharmacal scan). The garbling reflects transcription-pipeline age, not the commenter's argument.
proposals.upstream_parent: age of original document / scanning-pipeline artifact

proposals.name: Institutional self-credentialing / founding-and-membership recitation
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the text includes a paragraph reciting the submitting organization's credentials -- e.g. founding year, membership count, or superlative claims like 'the world's largest' or 'the oldest and largest'. 0 = no such credentialing language, 10 = an extensive, multi-sentence recitation of institutional credentials. Do NOT judge whether the organization actually is prestigious or whether this makes the comment better -- score only the extent of the credentialing language present in the text.
proposals.rationale: Multiple dense-favored items open with an extended credentialing paragraph before any substantive argument: R04 CAPA calls itself 'the world's largest professional pilot trade association,' R11 Boeing calls itself 'the world's largest manufacturer of commercial jetliners,' R43 ASSE calls itself 'the oldest and largest society of safety professionals.' This recites institutional reputation/seniority rather than engaging the rule.

proposals.name: Law-firm / outside-counsel representation markers
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the text shows markers of being drafted by outside legal counsel on behalf of a client -- e.g. an 'LLP' or law-firm name in the letterhead, multiple attorney names and/or multiple office addresses listed, or phrasing like 'on behalf of [client]' introducing the firm as drafter. 0 = no such markers, 10 = extensive law-firm letterhead/representation markers. Do NOT judge whether legal representation improves the comment's substance -- score only the extent of these markers.
proposals.rationale: Law-firm representation markers appear specifically in dense-favored items: R03 is filed by 'Eversheds Sutherland (US) LLP' with a named partner and office address; R16 lists roughly twenty attorney names across four offices ('Sonosky, Chambers, Sachse, Endreson & Perry, LLP'). This signals who drafted the comment (professional counsel), which is upstream of and separable from the argument's actual merit.

proposals.name: Coalition or third-party endorsement / 'joined by' language
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the text explicitly frames the comment as coordinated with, endorsing, or joining another party's separately filed comments -- e.g. 'I concur with the comments posted by X', '[Organization] is joined in these comments by [other organization]', or expressing support for a named third party's submission. 0 = the comment reads as an independent, self-contained submission with no such framing, 10 = the comment is explicitly and primarily framed as joining/endorsing another party's position. Do NOT judge whether coordinated advocacy is more or less credible -- score only the extent of this framing.
proposals.rationale: Explicit coalition/endorsement framing appears in this slice as a distinct, scorable channel: R19 ('I ... concur with the supporting comments posted by the NWPB's President and Vice President'), R14 ('NHA is joined in these comments by the Northwest Hydroelectric Association'), and R25 ('I want to express my support for the League of American Bicyclists' comments'). This flags participation in an organized campaign rather than an independently authored argument.

proposals.name: Procedural-only request (extension, scheduling, logistics)
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the comment's content is a purely procedural request -- e.g. a request to extend the comment period, a scheduling or logistics question, or a request for clarification about process -- rather than substantive engagement with the rule's provisions. 0 = comment is entirely substantive engagement with the rule's merits, 10 = comment is entirely a procedural request with no substantive engagement. Do NOT judge whether the procedural request is reasonable or well-justified -- score only the extent to which the content is procedural rather than substantive.
proposals.rationale: Some items are purely procedural and never engage the rule's merits: R17 (ACC/CBC's entire text is a 30-day extension request) and R54 (Philip Morris's entire text is a 90-day extension request); R56 (ALPA's one-line 'IN SUPPORT' AD comment) is similarly minimal engagement. Whether a comment is procedural-only is a strong, easily-scored predictor independent of substantive quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission-timing pressure on the commenter's internal review process

proposals.name: Footnote and formal legal-citation density
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the text uses formal legal-citation apparatus -- numbered footnotes, and/or pin-cites to statutes, regulations, or the Federal Register (e.g. 'U.S.C.', 'C.F.R.', 'Fed. Reg.'). 0 = no such citations or footnotes, 10 = dense, extensive footnoting/citation throughout. Do NOT judge whether the citations are accurate or persuasive -- score only the extent of the citation apparatus present.
proposals.rationale: Footnote/citation density is concentrated in dense-favored organizational filings: R14 (NHA, footnotes 1-2 with Fed. Reg. pin-cites), R33 (NASW, three numbered footnotes citing prior letters), R55 (Campaign for Tobacco-Free Kids, footnotes 1-3 citing NSDUH data). This tracks professional drafting convention, not argument strength.
proposals.upstream_parent: professional editing / legal training of drafter

proposals.name: Typographic emphasis intensity (all-caps, exclamation marks)
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the text uses typographic emphasis markers -- words in ALL CAPS, exclamation points, or repeated emphatic punctuation -- to convey urgency or emotion. 0 = no such emphasis markers, 10 = frequent and heavy use throughout. Do NOT judge whether the emotional tone is appropriate or persuasive -- score only the extent of the typographic emphasis markers.
proposals.rationale: Typographic emphasis appears mostly in card-favored personal comments: R01 uses 'strongly SUPPORT' in caps, R25 repeats 'EVERYONE' and 'SO MANY' in caps, and R45 is written almost entirely in emphatic, run-on caps-laden prose. This is a register/affect marker, not a quality marker.

proposals.name: Provision-level issue diagnosis
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment pinpoints specific provisions, paragraphs, definitions, or requirements and explains the precise problem; score 0 when it discusses only the proposal generally.
proposals.rationale: R02, R30, and R58 identify exact technical provisions, while R20 and R55 remain broadly supportive or oppositional without locating a specific provision.

proposals.name: Mechanism-based impact analysis
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment explains a clear causal chain from the proposed change to concrete effects; score 0 when it merely asserts that the change is good, bad, burdensome, or harmful.
proposals.rationale: R19, R24, and R51 connect regulatory choices to specific safety, health, or manufacturing effects, unlike the largely conclusory claims in R13 and R20.

proposals.name: Evidence traceability
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when claims are tied to identifiable studies, statutes, datasets, reports, or other sources and the sources are meaningfully interpreted; score 0 when citations are absent, vague, or merely decorative.
proposals.rationale: R03, R19, R24, and R26 integrate named evidence into their reasoning, whereas R15 and R55 make factual assertions with limited source traceability.

proposals.name: Interpreted quantitative support
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when relevant numbers are accurate-looking, clearly defined, and used to support a conclusion; score 0 when numerical claims are absent, unexplained, irrelevant, or presented without a logical connection.
proposals.rationale: R18, R19, R24, and R49 use quantities to frame regulatory effects, while R13 and R15 present numbers or estimates without adequately connecting them to the requested action.

proposals.name: Operational implementation realism
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment describes how compliance would work in practice, including timing, equipment, records, workflows, or failure modes; score 0 when it addresses only abstract policy goals.
proposals.rationale: R28, R30, R32, and R36 discuss concrete maintenance, testing, documentation, and implementation problems that are absent from generic comments such as R20 and R55.
